extracted.intended_audience: policy advocates, administrative law scholars, public-interest economists, and regulatory lawyers
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for producing scholarship, litigation briefs, regulatory comments, and advocacy that use economic analysis (especially the social cost of carbon) to influence environmental and other regulatory policy. Focuses on analytic rigor, litigation strategy, coalition-building, public communication, and training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish scholarship on critical policy issues
rubrics_metrics.description: To publish scholarship on critical policy issues; staff members have published an array of influential articles, books, and reports aimed at better quantifying the benefits of environmental policies and using this information rationally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholarship should be empirical/theoretical work that quantifies benefits (e.g., climate damages), appears in leading academic journals, and forms the foundation for advocacy; examples include work published in Nature and Science and co-authorship with leading economists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use economic analysis as an advocate’s tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic analysis can be an advocate’s most powerful tool, since a balanced look at the numbers often supports strong government protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocacy should build on rigorous economic work so arguments are grounded in quantified costs/benefits rather than solely normative claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ the Social Cost of Carbon (SCC) appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: The SCC is the best existing tool for assessing climate policies; work should defend the best current estimate (e.g., the Interagency Working Group value) and seek improvements by accounting for currently omitted damage categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use SCC in regulatory analysis, litigation, and comments; improve estimation methods and urge agencies to incorporate broader damage categories; examples include submissions to the National Academies and state guidance on SCC use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submit public comments on all relevant regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead and participate in coalitions submitting public comments on all federal regulations that affect greenhouse gas emissions, using arguments from scholarship to encourage proper use of the SCC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate with major environmental groups to ensure unified, sophisticated economic arguments in federal proceedings; use comments to build capacity of partner organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: File amicus briefs leveraging scholarship
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage academic and analytic expertise in amicus briefs to influence litigation outcomes and develop legal arguments not advanced elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop detailed, novel legal and economic arguments (e.g., historical regulatory practice, administrative-law sequencing) that can shape bench questioning and opinions; examples: briefs cited by courts in Zero Zone, Utility Air, EME Homer City, Michigan v. EPA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure agency analyses account for greenhouse gas impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal agencies must account for greenhouse gas impacts in their decisionmaking; analyses should include thorough greenhouse gas emissions analysis and avoid flawed assumptions like perfect substitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenge inadequate agency analyses in litigation and comments; show why assumptions (e.g., perfect substitution) run counter to basic economic principles and lead to irrational outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inappropriate speculation; model substitution effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on speculative claims (e.g., that new oil/gas leases reduce global emissions through fuel substitution); instead, model substitution effects so decisionmakers can fully consider consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage agencies to quantitatively model likely market and demand responses (including potential emission increases from price effects) rather than asserting substitution qualitatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider alternative development scenarios and leasing alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: NEPA and leasing analyses should analyze alternative development scenarios that best reduce environmental and social harms and account for option value of irreversible drilling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require rigorous consideration of alternatives, including delayed leasing or alternative uses, and quantify tradeoffs to inform decisions; cite failures where agencies omitted such analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate option value in natural-resource leasing decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Leasing decisions for federal natural resources should account for 'option value'—the value of delaying irreversible decisions to gain information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use real-option concepts in economic analyses and comments to justify delayed or more cautious leasing, higher minimum bids, or protection of sensitive areas; cite academic articles and litigation (e.g., Center for Sustainable Economy v. Jewell).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetize environmental externalities in energy policy
rubrics_metrics.description: State and federal electricity and distributed energy policy should monetize greenhouse gas and conventional air pollution impacts to evaluate policies appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop and advocate for methods (e.g., value of distributed energy resources) that monetize environmental impacts in planning and cost-effectiveness tests; participate in stakeholder working groups and regulatory proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground regulatory arguments in administrative-law precedent and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal arguments about agency authority and regulatory design should be informed by administrative-law history and institutional structure (e.g., how costs are assessed across regulatory stages; precedents for EPA's broader regulatory reach).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical and doctrinal analysis to show consistency or deviation from precedent; craft arguments about sequencing and the feasibility of cost assessment at different stages (cited in Michigan v. EPA and Clean Power Plan debates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocate methodological improvements to regulatory review
rubrics_metrics.description: Promote commonsense reforms to regulatory review such as improved retrospective review, independent agency review, and updated methodology guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compile consensus recommendations from former regulators and publish reports that offer implementable reforms for future administrations (example: Strengthening Regulatory Review report).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring economic arguments beyond environmental issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply cost-benefit reasoning and properly conducted economic analysis to non-environmental regulatory issues (e.g., Title X, predatory lending, public health, housing, net neutrality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit comments and amicus briefs across issue areas to ensure costs and benefits are properly considered; examples include litigation and comments in health and financial regulation contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use public communication and media strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish op-eds, speak to journalists, and provide data-driven roundups to shape public conversation and draw attention to policy and legal shortcomings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage high-profile outlets to highlight analytic findings (e.g., op-eds in NYT, Washington Post, LA Times) and public data (e.g., court win/loss roundups) to influence policymakers and the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build coalitions and capacity among advocacy organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Assemble and lead coalitions of environmental and other groups so influential organizations speak with a unified voice and use sophisticated economic arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide technical support, training, and co-authored comments to elevate partners' analytic capabilities and extend influence across federal and state proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train practitioners via clinics and fellowships
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer clinical education and fellowship programs that teach regulatory policy, economics, administrative law, and advocacy techniques, prioritizing internalization of externalities and properly conducted economic analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide hands-on student and fellow experience drafting comments, amicus briefs, and policy research; the clinics and fellowships should prepare alumni for government, academia, and advocacy careers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce data-driven, replicable analyses for litigation and policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Create analyses and briefs that are empirically grounded, replicable, and suitable for submission in litigation and rulemaking, supporting landmark court decisions and regulatory changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure briefs and comments contain sustained, detailed treatment of contested analytic issues (example: sustained discussion of SCC in Zero Zone amicus brief) so courts and agencies can rely on them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defend policies using economic and legal expertise when challenged
rubrics_metrics.description: When programs based on economic valuation (e.g., SCC-based programs) are litigated, combine legal and economic arguments to defend their design and implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare amicus briefs, expert reports, and litigation support that tie economic valuation to statutory interpretation and administrative reasonableness; examples include defense of New York's Zero Emission Credit program.
